docs.title: Handle errors
docs.heading_path: Claimable Neon for agents > Handle errors
docs.snippet: Every error has an error.code, human-readable error.message, error.origin, error.retryable, and error.request_id. Use the code for control flow. Retry only when error.retryable is true.

docs.title: Neon Pricing Plans
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans
docs.snippet: > Postgres Database, Authentication, and more backend primitives coming soon with three plans: Free, Launch, and Scale. Pay only for what you use on paid plans; no monthly minimum.

docs.title: How billing works
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > How billing works
docs.snippet: Paid plans are pay-as-you-go: usage is metered hourly and billed at the end of the month, with no monthly minimum. Plans apply per **organization**, and one Neon account can belong to multiple orgs on different plans. The Free plan is permanent (not a trial); no credit card…

docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Plans at a glance
docs.snippet: Plans at a glance

docs.title: Plans at a glance
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Plans at a glance

docs.title: Plans at a glance
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Plans at a glance
docs.snippet: All plans include: multi-AZ storage, autoscaling, database branching, read replicas, connection pooling, Postgres extensions (pgvector, PostGIS, TimescaleDB, and more), full management API and CLI, and a Data API for querying over HTTP.

docs.title: Table clarifications
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Table clarifications
docs.snippet: - **Branches** are capped at 5,000 per project on paid plans (10/25 included). Free is capped at 10 per project. - **Instant restore** is charged only on root branches; child branches don't add to this charge. - **Storage size** has no hard per-branch size limit on paid plans;…

docs.title: How can I try Neon without signing up?
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Common questions > How can I try Neon without signing up?
docs.snippet: Use Claimable Neon for an instant project, with no signup and no card. Provision from that page or the API. Claim it to a Neon account before expiration to keep it.

docs.title: What is a project?
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Common questions > What is a project?
docs.snippet: Your top-level container: primary database, branches, compute. Like a Git repo, with one project and many branches. Projects belong to **organizations**, where plans and billing apply.

docs.title: How are extra branches billed?
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Common questions > How are extra branches billed?
docs.snippet: Branches above your plan's allowance (10 included on Free/Launch, 25 on Scale) are billed at $1.50/branch-month, prorated hourly (~$0.002/hour). Example: 2 extra branches kept for 5 hours each = 10 branch-hours × $0.002 = $0.02.

docs.title: What happens when I hit Free plan limits?
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Common questions > What happens when I hit Free plan limits?
docs.snippet: Hitting any Free monthly limit (100 CU-hours, 0.5 GB storage, 5 GB egress) suspends compute until the next billing month. Upgrade to Launch or Scale to resume immediately.

docs.title: How can I control my costs?
docs.heading_path: Neon Pricing Plans > Common questions > How can I control my costs?
docs.snippet: See Cost optimization for the full guide and Reduce network transfer costs for egress.

docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method
docs.snippet: Your connection method depends on where your code runs. Use the table below for a quick lookup, or read the scenario sections for detailed guidance.

docs.title: Quick reference by environment

docs.snippet: Quick reference by environment

docs.title: Not using JavaScript or TypeScript?
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Find your scenario > Not using JavaScript or TypeScript?
docs.snippet: Use a standard TCP-based Postgres driver with a pooled connection. Connect from a secure backend server using your language's native driver.

docs.title: Running on a long-lived server (JS/TS)?
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Find your scenario > Running on a long-lived server (JS/TS)?
docs.snippet: If you deploy a JavaScript or TypeScript app to Railway, Render, a VPS, Docker, or any self-hosted environment with persistent processes, use a standard TCP driver with connection pooling. Your server can maintain a connection pool across requests, making TCP the fastest and…

docs.title: Deploying to Vercel or Cloudflare with platform pooling?
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Find your scenario > Deploying to Vercel or Cloudflare with platform pooling?
docs.snippet: These platforms provide their own connection pooling, which makes standard TCP the best choice.

docs.title: Deploying to another serverless or edge platform?
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Find your scenario > Deploying to another serverless or edge platform?
docs.snippet: For platforms like Netlify Functions, Deno Deploy, or Cloudflare Workers (without Hyperdrive), use the Neon serverless driver (@neondatabase/serverless). It connects over HTTP or WebSockets instead of TCP, reducing connection setup latency.

docs.title: Building a client-side app without a backend?
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Find your scenario > Building a client-side app without a backend?
docs.snippet: Use the Neon Data API via @neondatabase/neon-js. Browsers cannot open TCP connections to Postgres, so the Data API provides a secure HTTP interface with Row-Level Security support.

docs.title: Pooled vs. direct connections
docs.heading_path: Choosing your connection method > Understanding the options > Pooled vs. direct connections
docs.snippet: A **pooled connection** routes traffic through PgBouncer, which manages a pool of reusable Postgres connections. Use pooled connections by default. They handle up to 10,000 concurrent client connections and work well for serverless apps and high-concurrency workloads.

docs.title: Direct
docs.heading_path: Direct
docs.snippet: Direct postgresql://user:pass@ep-cool-rain-123456.us-east-2.aws.neon.tech/neondb?sslmode=require&channel_binding=require

docs.title: HTTP vs. WebSocket (serverless driver)
docs.heading_path: Direct > HTTP vs. WebSocket (serverless driver)
docs.snippet: - **HTTP** uses fetch requests. It is faster for single queries (~3 round trips vs. ~8 for TCP) and supports non-interactive transactions. Choose HTTP when your queries are independent, one-shot operations. - **WebSocket** maintains a persistent connection within a request. It…

docs.title: Data API
docs.heading_path: Direct > Data API
docs.snippet: The Data API provides a REST interface to your database over HTTP. It works in browsers, edge runtimes, and anywhere you can make HTTP requests. It validates JWTs from any authentication provider and enforces PostgreSQL Row-Level Security, making it suitable for client-side apps…

docs.title: ORM compatibility
docs.heading_path: Direct > ORM compatibility
docs.snippet: Popular JavaScript and TypeScript ORMs work with Neon across all connection methods. For non-JS/TS ORMs (Django, SQLAlchemy, ActiveRecord, Ecto), use your language's native Postgres driver with a pooled connection.

docs.title: The endpoint ID is not specified
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified
docs.snippet: With older clients and some native Postgres clients, you may receive the following error when attempting to connect to Neon:

docs.title: A. Pass the endpoint ID as an option
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified > A. Pass the endpoint ID as an option
docs.snippet: Neon supports a connection option named endpoint, which you can use to identify the compute you are connecting to. Specifically, you can add options=endpoint%3D[endpoint_id] as a parameter to your connection string, as shown in the example below. The %3D is a URL-encoded = sign.…

docs.title: B. Use libpq key=value syntax in the database field
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified > B. Use libpq key=value syntax in the database field
docs.snippet: If your application or client is based on libpq but you cannot upgrade the library, such as when the library is compiled inside of a an application, you can take advantage of the fact that libpq permits adding options to the database name. So, in addition to the database name,…

docs.title: C. Set verify-full for golang-based clients
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified > C. Set verify-full for golang-based clients
docs.snippet: If your application or service uses golang Postgres clients like pgx and lib/pg, you can set sslmode=verify-full, which causes SNI information to be sent when you connect. Most likely, this behavior is not intended but happens inadvertently due to the golang's TLS library API…

docs.title: D. Specify the endpoint ID in the password field
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified > D. Specify the endpoint ID in the password field
docs.snippet: Another supported workaround involves specifying the endpoint ID in the password field. So, instead of specifying only your password, you provide a string consisting of the endpoint option and your password, separated by a semicolon (;) or dollar sign character ($), as shown in…

docs.title: Libraries
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The endpoint ID is not specified > Libraries
docs.snippet: Clients on the list of drivers on the PostgreSQL community wiki that use your system's libpq library should work if your libpq version is >= 14.

docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Couldn't connect to compute node
docs.snippet: This error arises when the Neon proxy, which accepts and handles connections from clients that use the Postgres protocol, fails to establish a connection with your compute. This issue sometimes occurs due to repeated connection attempts during the compute's restart phase after…

docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Terminating connection due to administrator command
docs.snippet: The terminating connection due to administrator command error is typically encountered when running a query from a connection that has sat idle long enough for the compute to suspend due to inactivity. Neon automatically suspends a compute after 5 minutes of inactivity, by…

docs.title: Unsupported startup parameter
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Unsupported startup parameter
docs.snippet: The error occurs when using a pooled Neon connection string with startup options that are not supported by PgBouncer. PgBouncer allows only startup parameters it can keep track of in startup packets. These include: client_encoding, datestyle, timezone,…

docs.title: You have exceeded the limit of concurrently active endpoints
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > You have exceeded the limit of concurrently active endpoints
docs.snippet: Neon limits concurrently active computes to prevent resource exhaustion. When you exceed the limit, additional computes beyond the limit will remain suspended and you will see this error when attempting to connect to them. You can suspend other active computes and try again.…

docs.title: Remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
docs.snippet: This error occurs when the maximum number of simultaneous database connections, defined by the Postgres max_connections setting, is reached.

docs.title: Relation not found
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Relation not found
docs.snippet: This error is often encountered when attempting to set the Postgres search_path session variable using a SET search_path statement over a pooled connection. For more information and workarounds, please see Connection pooling in transaction mode.

docs.title: cannot execute ... in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > cannot execute ... in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)
docs.snippet: You attempted a write (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, COPY ... FROM, or DDL such as CREATE, ALTER, DROP, or TRUNCATE) in a transaction that Postgres treats as read-only. The error looks like this:

docs.title: Postgrex: DBConnection ConnectionError ssl send: closed
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Postgrex: DBConnection ConnectionError ssl send: closed
docs.snippet: Postgrex has an :idle_interval connection parameter that defines an interval for pinging connections after a period of inactivity. The default setting is 1000ms. If you rely on Neon's Scale to Zero feature (auto-suspend) to scale your compute to zero when your database is not…

docs.title: query_wait_timeout SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > query_wait_timeout SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly
docs.snippet: The query_wait_timeout setting is a PgBouncer configuration option that determines the maximum time a query can wait in the queue before being executed. Neon's default value for this setting is **120 seconds**. If a query exceeds this timeout while in the queue, it will not be…

docs.title: The request could not be authorized due to an internal error
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > The request could not be authorized due to an internal error
docs.snippet: This error page in the Neon Console is most often the result of attempting to access a Neon project in one browser window after you've have logged in under a different Neon user account from another browser window. The error occurs because the currently logged in Neon user…

docs.title: Terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout
docs.snippet: This error occurs when a session remains idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified timeout period. By default, the idle_in_transaction_session_timeout setting is set to 5min (300,000 milliseconds). This timeout helps prevent idle sessions from holding locks…

docs.title: Error connecting to database: Failed to fetch
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > Error connecting to database: Failed to fetch
docs.snippet: This error appears on the **Tables** page in the Neon Console when the Console's request to your compute doesn't complete:

docs.title: DNS resolution issues
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > DNS resolution issues
docs.snippet: Some users encounter DNS resolution failures when connecting to their Neon database. These issues are often reported when using the **Tables** page in the Neon Console. In such cases, users may see an **Unexpected error happened** message like the one below:

docs.title: DNS resolution issues
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > DNS resolution issues
docs.snippet: - Regional DNS caching or propagation delays - Restrictive or misconfigured DNS resolvers (such as those provided by your ISP) - System-wide web proxy settings that interfere with DNS resolution

docs.title: DNS resolution issues
docs.heading_path: Connection errors > DNS resolution issues
docs.snippet: Using a VPN routes DNS queries through a different resolver and often bypasses the issue entirely.

docs.title: Top level overview
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Top level overview
docs.snippet: Instead of running Postgres as a single stateful system tied to a VM and its filesystem, Lakebase Postgres is a serverless database that splits the system into two independent layers: compute and storage. These layers communicate over the network, with a stream of write-ahead…

docs.title: Resource hierarchy
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Resource hierarchy
docs.snippet: While the sections below describe the physical architecture, Lakebase Postgres on Neon organizes resources into a logical hierarchy:

docs.title: Compute layer
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Compute layer
docs.snippet: The compute layer is where Postgres actually runs. Each Lakebase Postgres compute node is a standard Postgres instance: it parses SQL, plans queries, executes transactions, enforces MVCC, and manages locks and indexes. From the perspective of the query engine, nothing about…

docs.title: Components
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Compute layer > Components
docs.snippet: - RAM - used for shared_buffers, session state, and hot data - Local NVMe - used as a performance cache for data pages

docs.title: How compute fits into the system
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Compute layer > How compute fits into the system
docs.snippet: - SQL is parsed and planned - Pages are accessed through the buffer manager - Changes are applied in memory

docs.title: Storage layer
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Storage layer
docs.snippet: If the compute layer is responsible for execution, the storage layer is responsible for correctness, durability, and history. **This layer exists independently of any single compute node and continues to operate even when computes come and go.**

docs.title: Safekeepers: defining correctness via WAL quorum
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Storage layer > Safekeepers: defining correctness via WAL quorum
docs.snippet: Safekeepers are responsible for one thing: **durable replication of WAL**. When a compute node generates WAL records, it streams them to multiple safekeepers. A transaction is considered committed once a quorum of safekeepers has acknowledged the WAL record via the Paxos…

docs.title: Pageserver: WAL ⇄ pages
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Storage layer > Pageserver: WAL ⇄ pages
docs.snippet: The pageserver sits between WAL and data pages. Its job is to **materialize page versions** by combining previously materialized base pages and committed WAL records. It is the system's translation layer between the logical history of the database and the physical representation…

docs.title: Object storage: long-term, immutable history
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Storage layer > Object storage: long-term, immutable history
docs.snippet: Object storage is where Lakebase Postgres keeps the **durable history** of the database. This layer stores materialized page versions, historical snapshots of data, and immutable representations of past states. It is not a query engine, and it is never accessed directly by the…

docs.title: Write path: committing a transaction
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Write path: committing a transaction
docs.snippet: 1. **Postgres applies changes in memory.** Rows are updated in shared buffers, indexes are modified, and WAL records are generated as usual. 2. **WAL is streamed to the safekeepers.** Instead of flushing WAL to a local filesystem, the compute node sends WAL records over the…

docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Read path: serving data without object-store latency
docs.snippet: The obvious concern with running a database on object storage is latency, but the lakebase architecture is designed specifically to avoid this. The most important thing to understand about reads is this: **queries do not read from object storage.** Object storage backs the…

docs.title: Durability
docs.heading_path: The lakebase architecture > Durability
docs.snippet: Durability in the lakebase architecture is not a single mechanism but a composition of responsibilities. No single component is responsible for everything, and no single machine defines the state of the database.

docs.title: Branching
docs.heading_path: Branching
docs.snippet: With Neon, you can quickly branch your data for development, testing, and various other purposes, enabling you to improve developer productivity and optimize continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipelines.

docs.title: What is a branch?
docs.heading_path: Branching > What is a branch?
docs.snippet: A branch is a copy-on-write clone of your data. You can create a branch from a current or past state. For example, you can create a branch that includes all data up to the current time or an earlier time.

docs.title: Development
docs.heading_path: Branching > Branching workflows > Development
docs.snippet: You can create a branch of your production database that developers are free to play with and modify. By default, branches are created with all of the data that existed in the parent branch, eliminating the setup time required to deploy and maintain a development database.

docs.title: Testing
docs.heading_path: Branching > Branching workflows > Testing
docs.snippet: Testers can create branches for testing schema changes, validating new queries, or testing potentially destructive queries before deploying them to production. A branch is isolated from its parent branch but has all of the parent branch's data up to the point of branch creation,…

docs.title: Temporary environments
docs.heading_path: Branching > Branching workflows > Temporary environments
docs.snippet: Create branches with TTL by setting an expiration date. Perfect for temporary development and testing environments that need automatic deletion.

docs.title: Restore and recover data
docs.heading_path: Branching > Restore and recover data
docs.snippet: If you lose data due to an unintended deletion or some other event, you can use **instant restore** to recover: roll the branch back to any point in time that still falls within your project's **history window** (the retention you configure under **Settings → Instant restore**).…

docs.title: History window
docs.heading_path: Branching > Restore and recover data > History window
docs.snippet: **Instant restore** (and Time Travel, branching from the past, and snapshots) need Neon to keep a log of data changes. The **history window** is the project-wide setting—on **Settings → Instant restore** in the Console—that controls how long that change history is retained,…

docs.title: Database branching workflow primer
docs.heading_path: Database branching workflow primer
docs.snippet: With Neon, you can work with your data just like you work with your code. The key is Neon's database branching feature, which lets you instantly create branches of your data that you can include in your workflow, as many branches as you need.

docs.snippet: If you're using GitHub Actions for your CI workflows, Neon provides GitHub Actions for creating, deleting, and resetting branches, and there's also a schema diff action.

docs.title: Development
docs.heading_path: Delete branch > A branch for every environment > Development
docs.snippet: You can create a Neon branch for every developer on your team. This ensures that every developer has an isolated environment that includes schemas and data. These branches are meant to be long-lived, so each developer can tailor their branch based on their needs. With Neon's…

docs.title: Preview environments
docs.heading_path: Delete branch > A branch for every environment > Preview environments
docs.snippet: Whenever you create a pull request, you can create a Neon branch for your preview deployment. This allows you to test your code changes and SQL migrations against production-like data.

docs.title: Testing
docs.heading_path: Delete branch > A branch for every environment > Testing
docs.snippet: When running automated tests that require a database, each test run can have its branch with its own compute resources. You can create a branch at the start of a test run and delete it at the end.

docs.title: Working with sensitive data
docs.heading_path: Delete branch > Additional branching features > Working with sensitive data
docs.snippet: If you're working with sensitive data and need to avoid copying production data to development or test environments, Neon supports schema-only branching. This creates branches with only the database schema (tables, indexes, constraints) without any of the actual data, allowing…

docs.title: Automatic branch cleanup
docs.heading_path: Delete branch > Additional branching features > Automatic branch cleanup
docs.snippet: To prevent branch accumulation and manage resources effectively, you can set branches to automatically expire and be deleted after a specified time period. This is a good fit for temporary environments like CI/CD test branches or time-limited preview deployments. See Branch…

docs.snippet: Production checklist

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Production checklist
docs.snippet: - [ ] 1. Use a paid plan for production workloads  Paid plans are usage-based, so your app won't stop or be limited as it grows. The Free plan includes compute hour limits, making it better suited for prototyping. - [ ] 2. Choose a region close to your application  Deploy your…

docs.title: Use a paid plan for production workloads
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Use a paid plan for production workloads
docs.snippet: Neon's paid plans are fully usage-based, which means your database is never subject to fixed limits that can stop your application as traffic grows. You pay for the compute and storage you use each month, without minimums.

docs.title: Choose a region close to your application
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Choose a region close to your application
docs.snippet: Network latency is one of the most common contributors to database response time: even a well-tuned database will feel slow if it's geographically far from your application servers. When creating a Neon project, choose the region that is closest to where your application runs.

docs.title: Keep your production branch as the default root branch
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Keep your production branch as the default root branch
docs.snippet: Your production database should run on a root branch that is set as the project's default branch. Neon projects are configured this way by default. Using a root branch enables snapshots, provides simpler billing (based on actual data size rather than accumulated changes), and…

docs.title: Protect your production branch
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Protect your production branch
docs.snippet: Neon makes it easy to branch, reset, and restore databases. In production, that power should be paired with explicit safeguards. Branch protection helps ensure that powerful features like restore, reset, and snapshot operations are used deliberately when applied to production…

docs.title: Enable autoscaling and set appropriate limits
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Enable autoscaling and set appropriate limits
docs.snippet: Neon autoscaling automatically adjusts compute resources based on your workload, allowing your database to absorb traffic spikes without manual intervention. For production workloads:

docs.title: Decide whether scale-to-zero is acceptable
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Decide whether scale-to-zero is acceptable
docs.snippet: Scale-to-zero allows Neon to suspend compute after a period of inactivity. This is a highly effective way to save costs in development environments and workloads with intermittent usage. For production workloads, the decision depends on your latency requirements.

docs.title: Test connection retries using the Neon API
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Test connection retries using the Neon API
docs.snippet: In a serverless architecture, brief connection interruptions can occur during scaling events or maintenance. Most database drivers and connection pools already implement retry logic for transient failures, but rather than assuming this works, you should test it.

docs.title: Size the history window for instant restore
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Size the history window for instant restore
docs.snippet: **Instant restore** lets you roll a branch's database timeline back in time. How far back you can go depends on the **history window** you configure (under **Settings → Instant restore**). On paid plans, the default history window is 1 day, which you can increase up to 30 days.

docs.title: Consider snapshot schedules
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Consider snapshot schedules
docs.snippet: Snapshot schedules provide regular, durable restore points taken daily, weekly, or monthly. While **instant restore** lets you roll back to any moment still inside your **history window**, snapshots capture stable points in time that you can return to later, ensuring that…

docs.title: Test your restore workflow
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Test your restore workflow
docs.snippet: Don't wait for an incident to learn how restore works. Plan and test your recovery process in advance.

docs.title: Clean up your branches regularly
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Clean up your branches regularly
docs.snippet: Neon's branching makes it easy to create preview, test, and temporary environments. Over time, unused branches can accumulate and contribute to unnecessary storage usage. To keep costs and complexity under control:

docs.title: Use pooled connections where they make sense
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Use pooled connections where they make sense
docs.snippet: Connection pooling increases the number of concurrent clients your database can serve (up to 10,000) by reusing a smaller number of backend connections. This reduces connection overhead and improves performance in web and serverless applications.

docs.title: Restrict access to production data
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Restrict access to production data
docs.snippet: Neon's IP Allow feature ensures that only trusted IP addresses can connect to your database, preventing unauthorized access and enhancing security. Combine an allowlist with protected branches for enhanced security.

docs.title: Install pg_stat_statements
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Install pg_stat_statements
docs.snippet: The pg_stat_statements extension provides query performance monitoring to track execution times and frequency. Since Neon doesn't log queries and has limited visibility into query performance, this extension helps you troubleshoot issues independently.

docs.title: Integrate with your existing observability stack
docs.heading_path: Getting ready for production > Integrate with your existing observability stack
docs.snippet: If you already operate an observability platform, you can export Neon metrics and logs to monitor database behavior alongside the rest of your system. This helps you:
